vignette: Kofi's memories of the war-torn streets of his childhood still lingered, a constant reminder of the fragility of life. As a park ranger in the United States, he had hoped to find solace in the tranquility of nature. But it was precisely this environment that now triggered the nightmares and flashbacks that had become an unwelcome companion. The rustling of leaves or the snapping of twigs transported him back to the sounds of gunfire and screams. The triggers were relentless - being criticised by his colleagues for not being vigilant enough, the sight of flames from a campfire, even the smell of smoke wafting through the forest. These reminders sent Kofi into a spiral of isolation, where he would cut off all contact with friends and family, avoiding social gatherings and meetings. He stopped wearing his uniform, unable to bear the similarity to the military fatigues that haunted his memories. Substance use became a coping mechanism - a way to numb the pain and quiet the voices in his head. But even in isolation, Kofi's mind was never at rest. Sleep problems plagued him, as he lay awake at night, anticipating threats that lurked in every shadow. He was convinced that something bad was happening whenever things took longer than expected - whether it was a delayed response from a colleague or a slower-than-usual hike through the woods. The constant hypervigilance left him exhausted and on edge. Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling of survival guilt, wondering why he had made it out alive when so many others hadn't. He felt isolated and set apart from others, as if his experiences had created an unbridgeable chasm between him and the world around him. The memories of what he had witnessed - and what he had done - continued to haunt him, violating the values he held dear. The more Kofi struggled with these negative appraisals, the more he perceived threats lurking in every corner. His isolation deepened, as he pushed away those who tried to get close to him. He became convinced that others saw him as damaged goods, unworthy of love or respect. The cycle was self-reinforcing - the more he isolated himself, the more he felt threatened, and the more he needed to escape into substance use. Kofi's avoidance behaviours had taken a toll on his relationships and work performance. His colleagues noticed the change in him, but Kofi couldn't bring himself to open up about what was happening. He felt like he was losing himself in the process of trying to cope with the trauma. It wasn't until Kofi hit rock bottom - waking up one morning after a particularly brutal nightmare, feeling completely disconnected from the world around him - that he knew he needed help. The thought of facing his demons head-on terrified him, but the prospect of living like this for the rest of his life was even more daunting. With a deep breath, Kofi picked up the phone and scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way out of the darkness that had consumed him.
